summary.text:
A book that did not move at all. Southend's PWLB debt stood at £339.332m at the start of 2025/26 and at exactly £339.332m at the end — no new loans, no maturities, in any of the four quarters — at an average 3.42%. 44% of it runs beyond thirty years. Total gross debt including invest-to-save financing and leases is £355.934m at 3.43%.

The movement is all on the other side. The CFR rose to £468.724m and internal borrowing to £112.790m, which is their own figure and reconciles exactly. Investments fell from £93.396m to £73.303m, and paragraph 7.6 is explicit about why: less in-house balance to invest 'as the Council seeks to delay borrowing for as long as possible'. Their own liability benchmark still shows loan debt above the gross loans requirement, so on that measure there is excess cash rather than a shortfall — but the direction of travel is one-way.

General Fund financing costs are 10.69% of net revenue stream against a revised budget of 10.37%. The £7.988m of Essex County Council transferred debt at 1.68% sits outside all of this, managed by the county and reimbursed.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual treasury report going to Cabinet on 7 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and this one is exact. We hold 50 PWLB loans for Southend totalling £339,332,266, against the £339.332m in your Tables 10 and 11 — the same figure you show at the start of 2025/26 and at the end of it, unchanged in all four quarters. No new loans, no maturities, all year. Your CFR of £468.724m less gross debt of £355.934m also gives the £112.790m of internal borrowing you state at 4.3, to the pound.

A book that does not move for twelve months is unusual enough to be worth a sentence, and it is not accidental — paragraph 7.6 is explicit that in-house balances are falling "as the Council seeks to delay borrowing for as long as possible". So the borrowing side has been held still deliberately while everything else moves: the CFR up, internal borrowing up to £112.790m, investments down from £93.396m to £73.303m.

Your own liability benchmark still shows loan debt outstanding of £346.920m against a gross loans requirement of £273.617m, which as your report says indicates excess cash rather than a shortfall. That is genuinely a comfortable position today. It is also, on the numbers in the same report, a one-way street — the two lines are converging from both ends, and the year in which they cross is the year the strategy has to change. That is precisely the question the liability benchmark exists to answer, and it is much easier to answer with a live curve behind it than annually.

For the moment that arrives: one-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26, five-year at 5.34%, ten-year at 5.83% and twenty-year at 6.38%, against the 3.42% your existing PWLB book costs. July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two other things. 44% of your borrowing runs beyond thirty years and only 6% falls due inside twelve months, so almost none of the existing book reprices on you — which is why the 3.42% has held. And on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, 37 of the 50 loans price below par for about £84.5m of net discount against 13 above par. Nothing follows from that on our side: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

Financing costs are 10.69% of net revenue stream against a 10.37% revised budget. And the £7.988m of Essex County Council transferred debt at 1.68% sits outside all of this as a deferred liability — we mention it only because it is easy to leave out of a comparison and then wonder why the averages don't tie.

On training, four fit Southend. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice is the one, given where your two lines are heading. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting sits next to it for the falling investment balance. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. And The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), written for members. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
